sense: a temporary departure from the normal
definition: A departure from what is normal, expected or typical, usually a brief or isolated one.
nuance: Aberration is used for a one-off oddity that does not fit the usual pattern: a result, a mood, a period of history. It often suggests the departure is temporary and will not be repeated. In science it also names a fault in how a lens focuses.

examples.text: The cold week in July was an aberration; the rest of the summer was hot and dry.
Historians argue that the dictatorship of the 1930s was an aberration, not the natural result of the country's past.
Her rude reply was an aberration; she is normally the politest person in the office.
The auditor flagged the sudden spike in spending as an aberration that needed an explanation.
He wondered whether the kindness she showed that evening was an aberration or a glimpse of her true self.
Odd readings can be dismissed as aberrations only if there is a clear reason to doubt the measurement.

cloze.text: One poor result in ten years is a temporary ___, not a sign that the whole school is failing.
The coach insisted that the heavy defeat was a one-off ___ and that his team was still the best in the league.
Compared with the long, peaceful decade before it, the riot that night looked like a strange ___ in the town's history.

misuse.text: Arriving late every single day became her usual aberration.
misuse.why: An aberration is a rare departure from the normal; something done every day is the norm.

misuse.text: The aberration of the two plans was clear, since they were almost identical.
misuse.why: An aberration is an odd departure from what is normal, not a difference between two things; 'similarity' or 'overlap' would fit.

phrases: This should be seen as an aberration, not a trend.
...was an aberration rather than the norm.

synonyms.vs: Anomaly is a neutral, technical word for anything that does not fit a pattern; aberration suggests a departure that is often temporary or regrettable.
Deviation is a neutral measure of difference from a standard; aberration implies something odd or wrong.

origin: From Latin aberrare, 'to wander away'.

sense: a ruler with cruel absolute power
definition: A ruler who holds absolute power and uses it cruelly or unfairly.
nuance: Despot is strongly disapproving. It describes rulers with unlimited power who oppress their people, and is sometimes used jokingly of a bossy boss or parent. Historians also speak of 'enlightened despots', who ruled absolutely but supported reform.

examples.text: The despot jailed anyone who criticised him and ruled the country for forty years without an election.
Some historians describe Catherine the Great as an enlightened despot who introduced reforms without sharing power.
My dad is a bit of a despot about the thermostat; nobody else is allowed to touch it.
International observers condemned the despot for ignoring every court ruling against him.
The village trembled whenever soldiers sent by the despot rode in, taking whatever grain they wanted.
Political theorists have long asked how societies can stop despots from seizing unlimited power.

cloze.text: The people finally overthrew the cruel ___ who had ruled them for decades without ever allowing a free vote.
A ___ answers to no parliament and no court: his word alone is law, and nobody may question it.
Not a gentle leader but a harsh ___, he punished every sign of opposition with prison or worse.

misuse.text: The despot was loved by his people because he shared power fairly with elected councils.
misuse.why: A despot holds absolute power and rules harshly, so sharing it fairly is the opposite.

misuse.text: She was a despot who gave her staff plenty of freedom and always asked for their opinions.
misuse.why: Despot suggests harsh, unchecked control, so it does not suit a friendly, open leader.

synonyms.vs: Tyrant stresses cruelty and abuse of power; despot stresses absolute, unchecked power.
Dictator is the usual political term for a ruler who seized power and keeps it; despot is more literary and stresses harshness.
Autocrat stresses ruling alone with total authority and need not suggest cruelty.

confusables.note: A depot is a storage place or a small bus or railway station; it sounds similar but means something else.

origin: From Greek despotes, 'master of a household'.

sense: a closing section after the main story
definition: A short section at the end of a book, play or film that tells what happened afterwards.
nuance: An epilogue sits after the main story and often jumps forward in time to show how things turned out. It is also used for a speech to the audience at the end of a play. Its opposite is the prologue, which comes at the start.

examples.text: I loved the book, but the epilogue, which jumps twenty years ahead to show what happened to everyone, felt rushed.
In the epilogue to his history of the war, the author reflects on how the peace was lost.
The documentary's epilogue reveals that the factory reopened last year, saving two hundred jobs.
The annual report ends with a short epilogue thanking the volunteers who made the year possible.
In the epilogue, the old soldier returns to the village and finds the orchard in bloom.
Shakespeare's The Tempest closes with an epilogue spoken directly to the audience.

cloze.text: The story had finished, but the final ___ told us who married whom and who went to prison.
Many novels open with a prologue and close with an ___ looking back from years later.
After the credits began, a short ___ explained what happened to the real family many years afterwards.

misuse.text: The epilogue of the book introduces the main characters and sets the scene.
misuse.why: An epilogue comes at the end; a section that introduces the story is a prologue.

misuse.text: The speech began with an epilogue about the history of the town.
misuse.why: An epilogue comes at the end of a work, so it cannot open a speech.

synonyms.vs: An afterword is a note about the book itself, often by the author; an epilogue continues the story.
A conclusion sums up an argument; an epilogue tells what came after the story.
Coda is a more poetic word for a closing passage, often shorter and borrowed from music.

confusables.note: An epitaph is the words written on a gravestone.
An epigraph is a short quotation placed at the start of a book.

origin: From Greek epilogos, 'the conclusion of a speech'.

sense: a story whose characters stand for ideas
definition: A story, poem or picture in which characters and events stand for ideas about morals or politics.
nuance: Allegory is used for works with a hidden second meaning that runs all the way through: each character or event stands for something else. It is common in literary and art criticism. Calling a work an allegory means it is meant to be read on two levels.

examples.text: Orwell's Animal Farm is an allegory: the pigs and horses stand for the leaders and workers of a real revolution.
The film is a simple allegory about greed, in which each character represents one of the seven deadly sins.
I thought it was just a story about a lost robot, but my teacher says it's an allegory about growing up.
The old woman told the children an allegory about a river that tried to flow uphill, and they understood her meaning.
Medieval writers loved allegories in which virtues and vices appeared as people.
The artist's mural is an allegory of justice, shown as a blindfolded woman holding scales.

cloze.text: Every character in the poem stands for a human weakness, so critics read it as a moral ___.
On the surface it is a tale about farm animals, but beneath it runs an ___ about political power.
The painting is not a portrait but an ___ of peace: the woman with the olive branch represents an idea, not a person.

misuse.text: The scientist wrote an allegory of the experiment, listing the methods and results in order.
misuse.why: An allegory tells a story with a hidden meaning; a plain report of methods and results is not one.

misuse.text: Tomorrow's weather forecast is a clear allegory of what will happen.
misuse.why: An allegory is a story whose parts stand for ideas, not a prediction; 'indication' or 'prediction' would fit.

phrases: The novel can be read as an allegory of...

synonyms.vs: A parable is a short, simple story that teaches a moral lesson; an allegory is usually longer and has many symbolic parts.
A fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson; an allegory carries a deeper meaning throughout.
A metaphor makes a comparison in a single phrase; an allegory extends the symbolism through a whole story.

confusables.note: An allergy is a bad reaction of the body to a substance; it sounds similar but is unrelated.

origin: From Greek allegoria, 'speaking otherwise', from allos, 'other', and agoreuein, 'to speak'.

sense: the methods and theory of teaching
definition: The methods and principles of teaching, and the study of how best to teach.
nuance: Pedagogy is used in education research and teacher training for how teaching is done and why. It covers choices such as lectures versus group work. It is a formal word and is rarely used for casual teaching.

examples.text: Teacher training courses spend a lot of time on pedagogy, the study of how best to teach different age groups.
The school adopted a new pedagogy that replaces long lectures with group projects.
My maths teacher's pedagogy is simple: let us struggle with a problem first, then explain the answer.
Research in pedagogy suggests that frequent short quizzes help students remember more.
The ministry published new guidance on pedagogy in early-years education.
The headmaster scorned modern pedagogies and still taught every lesson by dictation.

cloze.text: Her research is not about what children learn but about ___: the methods teachers use to help them learn it.
The training college teaches both the subject and the ___ of passing it on to young pupils.
Critics argue that the new ___ of rote repetition suits exam practice but does little for curiosity.

misuse.text: The pedagogy built the school's new library and sports hall.
misuse.why: Pedagogy is the method or study of teaching, not a person or a builder.

misuse.text: He studied pedagogy to become a doctor.
misuse.why: Pedagogy is about teaching methods; a doctor studies medicine.

synonyms.vs: Teaching is everyday and covers the act of doing it; pedagogy is the method and theory behind it.
Instruction is the delivery of lessons or directions; pedagogy is the thinking about how best to deliver them.

confusables.note: Demagogy is winning power by appealing to people's fears and prejudices; it looks similar but is unrelated to teaching.

origin: From Greek paidagogos, a slave who led children to school, from pais, 'child', and agein, 'to lead'.

sense: a value far from the rest of the data
definition: A value or case that lies far from the others in a set of results.
nuance: In statistics an outlier is a data point far from the rest, which may be a mistake or a real but unusual case. Researchers must decide whether to keep or remove it. It is also used more widely for any person or thing that stands apart from a group.

examples.text: One house in the survey sold for ten times the average price, so it was an outlier and was left off the graph.
Officials said the single hospital with high infection rates was an outlier and not part of a wider trend.
Our school's exam results were awful one year, but that was an outlier; they're fine now.
The committee asked analysts to explain each outlier before accepting the overall figures.
At a school full of bankers' children, she was the outlier, arriving each day in her brother's old coat.
Outliers can distort an average, so researchers must decide whether to keep them in the analysis.

cloze.text: Nine of the ten test scores were close together, but one was far higher, so it was treated as an ___ and checked.
The scientists removed the ___ because a faulty sensor had produced a reading far outside the normal range.
Among so many ordinary results, the one extreme score stood out as a clear ___.

misuse.text: The outlier of the team is the captain, because he stands in the centre of the group.
misuse.why: An outlier lies far from the rest, not in the middle.

misuse.text: She was an outlier on the committee because she agreed with everyone on every point.
misuse.why: An outlier stands apart from the group; someone who agrees with everyone fits in.

phrases: This result is a clear outlier, and...

synonyms.vs: Anomaly is any departure from what is expected; outlier is specifically a value far from the others in a set.
An exception breaks a rule or pattern; an outlier lies far from the cluster of results.

sense: courage to endure pain or hardship
definition: Courage and strength of mind that lets a person bear pain, loss or hardship calmly.
nuance: Fortitude is quiet, patient courage in the face of suffering or long difficulty, rather than bravery in a sudden danger. It is an approving word, often used of people facing illness, grief or hardship. In older writing it is one of the four cardinal virtues.

examples.text: My grandmother bore years of pain with such fortitude that most of us never knew how much she suffered.
The mayor praised the fortitude of residents who rebuilt their homes after the floods.
Medieval thinkers listed fortitude among the four cardinal virtues, alongside prudence, justice and temperance.
The award recognises the fortitude shown by volunteers who worked through the winter in difficult conditions.
It took all her fortitude to sit through the long night, waiting for news from the sea.
Studies of polar explorers often stress physical fortitude as much as technical skill.

cloze.text: Not a sudden act of daring but quiet ___ carried her through three long years of treatment.
Climbing through the storm demanded great mental ___ as well as physical strength, because the suffering lasted for hours.
The nurses showed remarkable ___, working calmly and patiently through months of grief and exhaustion.

misuse.text: He showed great fortitude by running away from the dog as fast as he could.
misuse.why: Fortitude is courage in enduring hardship; running away in a panic is not that.

misuse.text: The fortitude of the soup was thick and creamy.
misuse.why: Fortitude names a quality of character, not the texture of food; 'consistency' would fit.

synonyms.vs: Courage covers bold action in the face of danger; fortitude stresses patient endurance of pain or hardship.
Resilience is the ability to recover; fortitude is the strength to bear a hardship while it is happening.
Perseverance means carrying on towards a goal; fortitude means bearing suffering calmly.

confusables.note: Fortuitous means happening by chance.
A forte is a person's strong point or talent.

origin: From Latin fortitudo, 'strength', from fortis, 'strong'.

definition: Up to now, or up to the time being discussed, usually before a change.
nuance: Hitherto is a formal, slightly old-fashioned word for a situation that lasted until now and has probably changed. It is common in history and academic writing, often before an adjective, as in 'hitherto unknown'. It looks back from the present, so it needs a past or perfect verb.

examples.text: Hitherto, scientists had assumed the disease spread only by touch; this study shows it can also travel through the air.
Divers have discovered a hitherto unknown cave system beneath the lake.
Oh, a hitherto hidden talent! Why did you never tell us you could play the piano?
The captain, hitherto calm, suddenly shouted at the crew to turn the ship around.
The agreement removes restrictions that had hitherto prevented foreign firms from trading in the region.
The archive revealed a hitherto neglected group of letters that changed how historians view the period.

cloze.text: The discovery revealed a ___ unknown species, one that no scientist had ever recorded before.
His behaviour had ___ been polite and quiet, which made the sudden outburst all the more shocking.
The new law lifts a ban that had ___ stopped students from working more than ten hours a week.

misuse.text: I will hitherto start my diet tomorrow morning.
misuse.why: Hitherto looks back to the time before now; it cannot refer to the future.

misuse.text: Hitherto, she is studying medicine at university.
misuse.why: Hitherto describes a past situation that has now changed, so it needs a past or perfect verb, not a present state.

synonyms.vs: Previously is everyday and neutral; hitherto is formal and implies that things are different now.
Heretofore is even more legal and old-fashioned; hitherto is more common in general writing.

confusables.note: Hither is an old word meaning 'to this place'; it is the first half of hitherto.

origin: From the old word 'hither', meaning 'to this place', plus 'to', so 'up to this point'.

definition: Very common or widespread, especially of something bad or unpleasant.
nuance: Rife is almost always used of unwelcome things such as rumours, corruption, disease or errors. It usually follows 'be' and often takes 'with', as in 'rife with errors'. It is stronger and more critical than 'common'.

examples.text: Rumours were rife in the village after the mayor disappeared for three days.
Early nineteenth-century cities were rife with disease because few had clean water or proper sewers.
Gossip is rife at my workplace; I swear everyone knows my business before I do.
The audit found that fraud was rife in the department's purchasing system.
The castle was rife with whispers of betrayal, and no one dared trust a neighbour.
Student essays on the topic are often rife with the same few errors in referencing.

cloze.text: Within hours of the announcement, speculation was ___ and every newsroom had a different theory.
Corruption was ___ in the old regime: almost every official took bribes.
The draft was ___ with spelling mistakes; there seemed to be at least one in every line.

misuse.text: The party was rife, so everyone enjoyed themselves.
misuse.why: Rife describes unwelcome things that are widespread, such as rumours or disease, not a pleasant event.

misuse.text: She felt rife of joy at the wonderful news.
misuse.why: Rife is for widespread unwelcome things and takes 'with'; it does not describe a person's joy.

synonyms.vs: Widespread is neutral and can be good or bad; rife is formal and nearly always negative.
Rampant suggests spreading out of control and is more vivid; rife stresses how common something is.
Prevalent is a neutral, technical word for common at a particular time; rife is more critical.

confusables.note: Ripe means fully grown and ready to eat or use.

definition: Useful or convenient for a particular aim, even if it is not quite fair or moral.
nuance: Expedient praises what works but hints that principle is being set aside: the choice is judged by convenience, not by what is right. It is common in politics, business and ethics essays. The word can also be a noun for a quick method.

examples.text: It was politically expedient for the minister to blame the previous government, even though he knew the facts were more complicated.
Machiavelli's The Prince is often read as advising rulers to do what is expedient rather than what is morally right.
Telling a little white lie was the expedient thing to do, but I felt guilty afterwards.
The board chose the expedient course of cutting training costs, which saved money this year but harmed the company later.
It would be expedient, he reasoned, to forget what he had seen in the cellar.
Critics argue that the treaty was an expedient arrangement that avoided war but solved none of the underlying disputes.

cloze.text: Cutting corners was ___ in the short term, saving time and money, but it was not right and it cost them later.
The mayor did what was politically ___ rather than what was fair, and everyone knew it.
Lying seemed the ___ choice: quick and convenient, though plainly dishonest.

misuse.text: The expedient delay of five years made the project slow and costly.
misuse.why: Expedient means convenient or quick for a purpose; a long, costly delay is not that.

misuse.text: She was a very expedient friend who always told the truth and helped others at her own cost.
misuse.why: Expedient suggests choosing what is convenient for oneself, often against principle, so it does not suit a selfless, honest friend.

phrases: It may be expedient to..., but it is not just.

synonyms.vs: Pragmatic is usually approving and about realism; expedient hints at convenience over principle.
Convenient is everyday and has no moral edge; expedient suggests the easy choice may be improper.
Advantageous means bringing benefit; expedient means serving an immediate aim whether or not it is right.

confusables.note: Expeditious means quick and efficient.
Expedite means to make a process happen sooner.

origin: From Latin expedire, 'to free the feet', so to make ready or useful.

sense: formal forgiveness or freedom from blame
definition: Formal forgiveness for a sin or wrongdoing, or a declaration that someone is free of blame.
nuance: Absolution began as a priest's forgiveness of sins after confession. It now also means being freed from blame or guilt, often in discussions of responsibility. It is usually 'granted', 'sought' or 'denied', and 'no absolution for...' is a common way to say someone remains to blame.

examples.text: After confessing to the priest, he knelt and received absolution, and the heavy guilt finally lifted from his shoulders.
Medieval Christians believed that absolution, given by a priest after confession, cleared the soul of sin.
The inquiry gave the company no absolution: it found that managers had ignored safety warnings for years.
I told her it was fine, but she kept apologising as if she needed absolution from me.
The report refused to grant absolution to any official who had known about the fraud and said nothing.
Some critics argue that charity gifts offer wealthy donors a kind of moral absolution without changing how they earn their money.

cloze.text: Kneeling in the church, she confessed her sins and hoped the priest would grant her ___.
Giving money to charity did not buy the tycoon ___ for the way he had treated his workers.
He sought ___ from his family, hoping they would release him from guilt and shame.

misuse.text: The judge gave the criminal an absolution of twenty years in prison.
misuse.why: Absolution frees someone from blame or sin; a prison sentence is a punishment.

misuse.text: She felt great absolution when she lost her keys again.
misuse.why: Absolution means forgiveness or freedom from blame, not annoyance at a loss.

phrases: The verdict amounted to absolution of...

synonyms.vs: Forgiveness is everyday and personal; absolution is formal, often official or religious, and clears blame.
A pardon is an official act cancelling a punishment; absolution frees someone from sin or blame.
Acquittal is a court's decision that someone is not guilty; absolution is wider and moral or religious.

confusables.note: Absolute means complete or total; it shares a Latin root but its meaning is different.

origin: From Latin absolvere, 'to set free', from ab-, 'from', and solvere, 'to loosen'.

definition: Going against the accepted beliefs of a religion or an established group.
nuance: Heretical began as a religious charge of false belief. It is now also used, seriously or playfully, for ideas that challenge a field's accepted wisdom. Whether it sounds bold or dangerous depends on the writer.

examples.text: The church condemned his teachings as heretical and forbade anyone to read his books.
In 1633 Galileo's claim that the Earth moves round the sun was judged heretical by Church authorities.
Putting ketchup on a perfectly cooked steak? That's practically heretical in my family.
The economist's heretical proposal to abolish the central bank shocked his colleagues but won him many readers.
The committee dismissed the paper as heretical, since it rejected the field's most basic assumptions.
At the time, such heretical ideas about the nature of the soul could lead to imprisonment.

cloze.text: Medieval inquisitors hunted down anyone whose religious opinions were ___, that is, opposed to official church teaching.
For a lifelong vegetarian to praise a steak would be almost ___ among his friends, a betrayal of their cherished belief.
Her ___ theory overturned the department's most sacred assumptions, and some colleagues refused to speak to her.

misuse.text: The heretical bus arrived on time and nobody complained.
misuse.why: Heretical describes ideas that go against accepted beliefs, not vehicles or events.

misuse.text: He was praised for his heretical loyalty to the church.
misuse.why: A heretical view opposes accepted doctrine, so it cannot mean loyalty to it.

phrases: At the time, such a view was considered heretical.

synonyms.vs: Heterodox is a formal, neutral word for opinions that differ from the accepted view; heretical sounds stronger and condemns.
Unorthodox describes unusual, non-traditional methods or opinions and need not break any rule of belief.
Blasphemous means insulting a god or sacred things; heretical means going against official teaching.

confusables.note: Hysterical means wildly emotional or extremely funny.

origin: From Greek hairesis, 'choice': a heretic picks his own belief over the accepted teaching.

definition: Fixed for ever and impossible to change.
nuance: Immutable describes laws, truths, facts and principles that are fixed. It is stronger than 'unchanging' because it says change is impossible. In social science it often appears in the claim that something supposedly immutable has in fact changed.

examples.text: Many early scientists believed that the laws of nature were immutable, fixed for all time.
The president said the country's borders were immutable and could never be redrawn.
My mum treats Sunday lunch as immutable; the whole family has to be there, no excuses.
The contract contains no immutable terms; both parties may ask to renegotiate after one year.
To the old king, the order of rank at court was immutable, as fixed as the stars.
Sociologists reject the idea that gender roles are immutable, pointing to how much they differ between cultures and centuries.

cloze.text: The rules of the game are ___: no player, however famous, can ever change them.
Nothing in life is truly ___; even mountains slowly wear away over millions of years.
Scientists treat the speed of light as a fixed and ___ feature of the universe, the same everywhere and for all time.

misuse.text: Her immutable moods changed every few minutes.
misuse.why: Immutable means impossible to change, the opposite of moods that change every few minutes.

misuse.text: The immutable paint peeled and faded within a year.
misuse.why: Immutable means unable to change; paint that peels and fades is changing.

synonyms.vs: Unchangeable is plain English; immutable is formal and often used of laws or truths.
Permanent means lasting for ever; immutable says it cannot be altered even if people try.
Fixed is everyday and may only mean not changing for now; immutable means it can never change.

confusables.note: Immovable means unable to be moved, or unwilling to change one's mind.
Immune means protected from a disease or an influence.

origin: From Latin immutabilis, 'unchangeable', from in-, 'not', and mutare, 'to change'.

definition: So clearly true that nobody can reasonably argue against it.
nuance: Indisputable is a strong word for facts and evidence that leave no room for doubt. It is common in argument, law and sports reporting. In an essay, use it sparingly: calling something indisputable invites readers to look for an exception.

examples.text: Her talent is indisputable; even her rivals admit she is the best player in the league.
The fossils provide indisputable evidence that birds are descended from dinosaurs.
The video offered indisputable proof of where the car had been at the time.
The facts are indisputable, though the committee interprets their meaning differently.
It was an indisputable fact that the house had been empty for years, yet the lights were on.
Few historians would call the economic effects of the policy indisputable, since the data are patchy.

cloze.text: The DNA match left no room for doubt, so the evidence was ___.
That the Earth orbits the Sun is an ___ fact; no serious scientist questions it.
Her gift for music is clear and ___; even her fiercest critics admit it.

misuse.text: The indisputable rumour was repeated by people who had no idea if it was true.
misuse.why: Indisputable means beyond doubt; a rumour nobody has checked cannot be indisputable.

misuse.text: It is indisputable that some people prefer tea, but others may disagree.
misuse.why: If others may disagree, it is not indisputable; the word claims that no reasonable disagreement is possible.

synonyms.vs: Undeniable is a little warmer and more common in speech; indisputable stresses that nobody can argue.
Incontrovertible is more formal and often used of evidence in law and science.
Irrefutable is about arguments or proofs that cannot be proved wrong; indisputable covers facts generally.

definition: A person who is rejected and avoided by others, treated as an outcast.
nuance: Pariah suggests someone shunned by a whole group or society, sometimes unfairly and sometimes for wrongdoing. It is also used for states, companies and ideas that others will have nothing to do with, as in 'pariah state'. It is strongly negative about the person's status.

examples.text: After the scandal, the businessman became a pariah, and former friends crossed the street to avoid him.
Isolated by sanctions, the regime became a pariah among nations, cut off from trade and diplomacy.
Since I told the boss about the missing money, I've felt like a pariah in the office.
The new girl sat alone at lunch every day, a pariah before she had said a single word.
The company risked being treated as a pariah by investors if it ignored the new rules.
Studies of prison life show how pariahs, such as informers, are shunned by other inmates.

cloze.text: Nobody would sit with him or speak to him; he had become a social ___, shunned by everyone.
The country was treated as a ___ by its neighbours after it broke the treaty, and no one would trade with it.
After her betrayal, she was a ___ in the village, ignored in the shop and avoided at church.

misuse.text: The pariah was the most popular person at the party, surrounded by friends.
misuse.why: A pariah is rejected and avoided by others, so being surrounded by friends is the opposite.

misuse.text: The mayor called the new park a pariah for the town.
misuse.why: Pariah describes an outcast person, group or state, not a place that people enjoy.

synonyms.vs: Outcast is more general and can be neutral or sympathetic; pariah stresses being shunned by a whole society.
Exile means forced to leave a place; a pariah may still live among those who avoid them.

definition: To grow and develop quickly, becoming larger, more numerous or more successful.
nuance: Burgeon suits things that increase fast and in a healthy way: cities, industries, talent, populations. It is most often seen as the adjective 'burgeoning'. The tone is positive or neutral, though fast growth can bring pressure.

examples.text: The burgeoning tech industry has turned the quiet harbour town into a busy city of cafes and start-ups.
Nineteenth-century factories drew workers into burgeoning cities that struggled to provide clean water.
My little sister has a burgeoning interest in astronomy; she now has three telescopes and two posters.
The ministry welcomed the burgeoning export trade, which had doubled in just four years.
In the spring the orchard burgeoned, and white blossom covered every branch within a week.
The field of data science burgeons whenever new technology makes huge collections of information cheap to store.

cloze.text: In the warm weather the garden began to ___, and green shoots sprang up everywhere within days.
The ___ population of the new town put heavy pressure on its schools and roads.
Since the film's release, her career has ___, with job offers arriving from three continents.

misuse.text: The village's population burgeoned as families moved away and the school closed.
misuse.why: Burgeon means to grow quickly; a shrinking population is the opposite.

misuse.text: She burgeoned her small business with a bank loan.
misuse.why: Burgeon has no object: a business can burgeon but you cannot burgeon it. Use 'expand' or 'grow' here.

synonyms.vs: Flourish means thrive and do well, without needing fast growth; burgeon stresses rapid increase.
Boom is informal and mainly about sudden economic growth; burgeon is more general and literary.
Proliferate means to multiply fast in number and can sound uncontrolled; burgeon is more positive.

confusables.note: Bludgeon means to beat with a heavy stick or to force someone into something.

origin: From Old French burjon, 'a bud', so to burgeon is to put out buds and grow.

definition: To teach someone a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they accept them without question.
nuance: Indoctrinate is disapproving: it means fixing beliefs in people's minds by repetition and pressure, not by encouraging them to think. It is used of schools, cults, regimes and sometimes advertising. Its opposite in spirit is 'educate'.

examples.text: The regime used schools to indoctrinate children, making them repeat slogans praising the leader every morning.
Critics argue that teaching only one version of history can indoctrinate pupils rather than educate them.
My parents never tried to indoctrinate me; they told me to read widely and make up my own mind.
Teachers are forbidden to indoctrinate pupils with any political or religious belief during lessons.
Indoctrinated since birth, the young soldier never questioned the orders that came from the tower.
Propaganda works by indoctrinating people with simple slogans until they repeat them without thought.

cloze.text: A good teacher helps pupils to think for themselves, whereas a propagandist tries to ___ them with fixed ideas.
The cult ___ its new members, repeating the same claims for hours until nobody dared to doubt them.
Children brought up in the sect were ___ from an early age to fear the outside world.

misuse.text: The teacher indoctrinated the class by encouraging them to question everything.
misuse.why: Indoctrinate means drilling beliefs in without question, so encouraging questions is the opposite.

misuse.text: He indoctrinated the cake with chocolate sauce.
misuse.why: Indoctrinate is about teaching people beliefs, not covering an object with something.

synonyms.vs: Brainwash is informal and stronger, suggesting force; indoctrinate is formal and often gradual, through teaching.
Educate is approving and encourages thinking; indoctrinate is critical and discourages it.
Condition suggests training someone to react automatically; indoctrinate is about fixing beliefs.

origin: From the noun doctrine, from Latin doctrina, 'teaching'.

sense: the highest point of success or power
definition: The highest point, especially the moment of greatest success, power or fame.
nuance: Zenith literally means the point in the sky directly overhead. In writing it names the high point of a career, empire, civilisation or trend, and it suggests that decline comes afterwards. It is common in the phrases 'reach its zenith' and 'at the zenith of'.

examples.text: The Roman Empire reached its zenith in the early second century, when its borders stretched from Britain to the Middle East.
Honestly, that tournament was the zenith of her career; she never played that well again.
At the zenith of his fame, the singer sold out stadiums in forty countries.
The company reached its zenith in 1999, then lost half its value within three years.
The sun stood at its zenith, directly overhead, and the street was empty of shade.
Many historians date the zenith of the Dutch Golden Age to the middle of the seventeenth century.

cloze.text: After years of climbing, the band reached the ___ of its fame, and then it split up.
At noon the sun reaches its ___, the highest point in the sky, and shadows almost vanish.
Winning the prize was the ___ of her career, and critics wondered if she could ever do better.

misuse.text: After the crash, the firm sank to its zenith and lost all its customers.
misuse.why: Zenith is the highest point; the lowest point is the nadir.

misuse.text: They celebrated the zenith of the project at its very beginning, when nothing had been built.
misuse.why: Zenith means the high point reached after growth, not the start of something.

phrases: At the zenith of its power,...

synonyms.vs: Peak is everyday and general; zenith is literary and suggests a final high point before decline.
Pinnacle suggests the top of an achievement; zenith more often marks the highest point of an era or power.
Apex is a neutral, geometric word for the top; zenith carries a sense of the grandest moment.

origin: From Arabic samt ar-ra's, 'the path over the head', through medieval Latin.

sense: seize power or a place wrongly
definition: To take a position, power or right by force or without having the right to it.
nuance: Usurp is used of power, thrones, roles and authority taken unlawfully or unfairly. It is common in history and politics, and lightly when a cat takes your chair. The usual objects are 'the throne', 'power', 'authority' and 'the role of'.

examples.text: The king's brother usurped the throne while the rightful heir was abroad, and had himself crowned within a week.
In Shakespeare's Macbeth, the hero usurps the crown by murder, and the play shows the cost of that crime.
Critics accused the president of usurping the powers of parliament by ruling through emergency decrees.
The cat has usurped my chair; she sits there all day and hisses when I come near.
The new rules must not usurp the authority of local councils to set their own budgets.
Some historians argue that television usurped the newspaper's role as the nation's main source of news.

cloze.text: The general tried to ___ the throne, though he had no legal claim to rule.
Parents worry that screens ___ the place once held by family conversation at dinner.
A minister who ignores the courts and acts alone ___ powers that belong to the whole parliament.

misuse.text: The prince usurped the throne after it was handed to him lawfully by his father.
misuse.why: To usurp is to take power without the right; a lawful handover is not usurping.

misuse.text: She usurped her grandmother a lovely birthday present.
misuse.why: Usurp means to seize a position or power wrongly; it cannot mean to give something.

synonyms.vs: Seize is everyday and works for anything; usurp is formal and suggests taking a position you have no right to.
Supplant means to replace, perhaps fairly; usurp means taking by force or without right.
Overthrow means removing a ruler from power; usurp means wrongly taking their place.

confusables.note: Usury is lending money at unfairly high interest.

definition: A person or thing that is a perfect or very good model of something and worth copying.
nuance: Exemplar is approving: it names the best or most typical case of a quality or type. In academic writing it also means a clear typical example used to explain an idea. It is formal; in everyday speech people say 'a model' or 'a perfect example'.

examples.text: The nurse was praised as an exemplar of kindness, staying long after her shift to comfort patients.
The novel is often taught as an exemplar of the detective genre because it follows every convention.
My grandfather was my exemplar of hard work; he never missed a day's work in forty years.
The school gave pupils an exemplar of a top-scoring essay so they could see what the markers wanted.
She was the exemplar of elegance, and every young woman in the room tried to copy her walk.
Researchers use exemplars, or clear typical cases, to explain abstract ideas to new students.

cloze.text: Held up as a perfect ___ of honesty, the judge was admired by lawyers and public alike.
For young cooks, the chef is an ___ to follow: calm, careful and endlessly patient.
Students received an ___ of a top-scoring answer, a model to show the standard they should aim for.

misuse.text: He exemplar honesty to all his pupils.
misuse.why: Exemplar is a noun meaning a model; the verb is 'exemplify'.

misuse.text: The exemplar was a rare insect found only in the north.
misuse.why: An exemplar is a model worth copying or a typical case, not a living specimen; 'specimen' would fit.

synonyms.vs: Model is everyday and wide; exemplar is formal and stresses a perfect, representative case.
Paragon is stronger and means a perfect example of a quality, usually a person.
Epitome means the perfect example of a type, whether good or bad; exemplar is mostly a good model.

confusables.note: Example is the everyday word for any case; exemplar is a formal word for a model worth copying.

sense: invent reasons to justify bad behaviour
definition: To find reasons that make a poor choice or bad behaviour seem sensible, often to avoid guilt.
nuance: Rationalise usually means making excuses to yourself: finding respectable reasons for something done for a different, less comfortable reason. It is a key idea in psychology. In business it can also mean reorganising to save money, but the excuse sense is the one met in essays. British English spells it rationalise; American English spells it rationalize.

examples.text: He rationalised buying a third pair of trainers by telling himself that the other two were nearly worn out, though both were almost new.
People often rationalise unhealthy habits by pointing to the one relative who smoked and lived to ninety.
The minister tried to rationalise the cuts as a way of protecting jobs, but few voters believed him.
It is tempting to rationalise a poor result after the event, but the review must look for real causes.
She rationalised her silence all the way home: it was not lying, she told herself, if nobody asked.
Psychologists describe how rationalising a decision afterwards helps people feel better about choices they regret.

cloze.text: Instead of admitting he was lazy, he tried to ___ missing the deadline by blaming the weather and the traffic.
It is easy to ___ a bad decision afterwards, inventing sensible-sounding reasons that were never in your mind at the time.
She ___ her overspending as 'an investment' so that she would not feel guilty about the bill.

misuse.text: She rationalised the cake by cutting it into eight equal slices.
misuse.why: To rationalise is to invent reasons that justify something, not to divide or share things equally.

misuse.text: He rationalised honestly that he had made a terrible mistake.
misuse.why: Rationalise means finding excuses to justify bad behaviour; admitting an error honestly is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Justify can be honest and sound; rationalise suggests the reasons are only excuses.
Excuse is everyday and about asking others to overlook a fault; rationalise is mainly about convincing yourself.
Explain away means dismissing a problem with clever reasons; rationalise stresses defending your own conduct.

confusables.note: A ration is a fixed share of something, or to limit supplies; it is a different idea from finding reasons.

definition: Friendly, pleasant and easy to get on with.
nuance: Amiable describes people, and their smiles, manner or talk, as pleasant and good-natured, without being intense. It is mild and warm, and can hint at a lack of edge or ambition. It is common in descriptions of character and in discussions that went well.

examples.text: The new neighbour was an amiable man who waved to everyone and always stopped for a chat.
Our dog is amiable with everyone; she would happily go home with a burglar.
The amiable captain chatted with fans for an hour after the match, signing every shirt they held out.
Reviewers described the narrator as amiable but unreliable, a pleasant companion who hides important facts.
The two delegations held an amiable discussion and parted on good terms.
Dickens fills his novels with amiable characters whose kindness stands against the cruelty of the age.

cloze.text: Everyone liked the ___ shop owner, who greeted every customer with a warm smile and remembered their names.
The meeting was ___ rather than tense; people laughed, listened and parted as friends.
Despite their different politics, the two neighbours kept up an ___ relationship over the garden fence.

misuse.text: The amiable dictator ordered the arrest of his critics.
misuse.why: Amiable means friendly and good-natured, which clashes with harshly arresting critics.

misuse.text: The amiable argument ended with shouting and slammed doors.
misuse.why: An amiable exchange is friendly and calm, so shouting and slamming doors is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Friendly is everyday; amiable is a little more formal and suggests an easy, good-natured temper.
Affable stresses being easy to talk to, especially for someone important; amiable is about general warmth.
Genial suggests a cheerful, welcoming manner, often in older people.

confusables.note: Amicable describes friendly relations between people or groups, as in an amicable divorce; amiable describes a person's nature.

definition: Existing or happening at the same time as something else, especially in the past.
nuance: Contemporaneous links two events, people or records from the same period. It is common in history, law and science, as in 'contemporaneous records'. Unlike 'contemporary', which usually means modern, it needs a second thing to compare with.

examples.text: The two painters were contemporaneous, working in the same Paris studios in the 1880s, so their styles often overlap.
The court accepted the diary as contemporaneous evidence because it was written on the day of the accident.
Police released contemporaneous notes taken by the officer at the scene.
Wait, were the dinosaurs and early humans contemporaneous? No, millions of years separate them.
The letter was contemporaneous with the fire; the date on it was the very night the house burned.
The rise in crime was contemporaneous with rising unemployment, but this does not show that one caused the other.

cloze.text: Historians value diaries written at the time because they are ___ records, not memories written years later.
The two kingdoms were ___ and shared the same century, though they never met.
The rise in ice-cream sales was ___ with an increase in sunburn, though the hot sun was the cause of both.

misuse.text: She loved contemporaneous art, such as the paintings of the past year.
misuse.why: Contemporaneous means happening at the same time as something else; for art of today use 'contemporary'.

misuse.text: The contemporaneous events followed each other over the next decade.
misuse.why: Contemporaneous means at the same time, not one after another.

synonyms.vs: Simultaneous suggests exactly the same moment; contemporaneous allows an overlapping period.
Concurrent is common in law and computing for things running together; contemporaneous is used for periods of history and records.
Coeval is rarer and literary; it means of the same age or era.

confusables.note: Contemporary usually means modern or of today; contemporaneous only means at the same time as something named.

sense: a vague feeling of unease or decline
definition: A general feeling of unease, weakness or dissatisfaction that is hard to explain.
nuance: Malaise covers a vague feeling of being unwell and, more often, a mood of discontent in a person, a group, a society or an economy. It is common in news and cultural analysis, as in 'economic malaise'. It is not a specific illness.

examples.text: I have a general malaise today: not ill exactly, just tired and flat, as if something is wrong.
Economists blame the long malaise in the housing market on high interest rates and falling confidence.
The poem captures the spiritual malaise of a generation that returned from war unable to believe in anything.
A strange malaise settled over the household after the funeral, and nobody could say what was wrong.
The survey found a deep malaise among staff, though no single complaint explained it.
Historians describe the 1970s as a period of national malaise, marked by strikes, inflation and loss of confidence.

cloze.text: After weeks of rain and bad news, a heavy ___ hung over the town, though nobody could say exactly why.
Falling morale, empty offices and constant complaints were all signs of a deeper ___ in the company.
The doctor found nothing wrong, but the patient still complained of a vague ___, a feeling of being unwell with no clear cause.

misuse.text: The malaise exploded with a loud bang and shattered the windows.
misuse.why: Malaise is a vague, spreading feeling of unease, not a sudden event.

misuse.text: She felt a joyful malaise when she won the lottery.
misuse.why: Malaise is a feeling of unease or dissatisfaction, so it cannot be joyful.

synonyms.vs: Unease is everyday and can be brief; malaise is more formal and suggests a lingering, spreading mood.
Discontent is clear dissatisfaction with something; malaise is vaguer and harder to explain.
Ennui is a literary feeling of boredom and weariness; malaise includes anxiety and decline.

confusables.note: Malice is the wish to harm someone.

origin: From French mal, 'bad', and aise, 'ease'.

sense: travelling from place to place for work
definition: Travelling from place to place, especially in order to find work.
nuance: Itinerant describes workers, preachers, traders, musicians and teachers who do not stay in one place. It is neutral, though it can suggest a hard, unsettled life. It can also be a noun for such a person.

examples.text: Itinerant farm workers follow the harvest from one region to the next, rarely staying anywhere for long.
An itinerant tinker arrived each spring, mending pots and trading stories for a night's lodging.
Medieval learning spread partly through itinerant scholars who travelled between monasteries and early universities.
My uncle led an itinerant life as a musician, living in a new city every year.
The charity supports itinerant teachers who bring lessons to children in remote communities.
In the eighteenth-century revivals, itinerant preachers carried their message from village to village.

cloze.text: The circus is run by an ___ company that packs up its tents and moves to a new town every week.
As a young man he worked as an ___ labourer, picking fruit in one county and building fences in the next.
Her ___ childhood, with a new school every year because her father kept changing jobs, left few lasting friendships.

misuse.text: The itinerant farmer spent his whole life on the same field.
misuse.why: Itinerant means travelling from place to place, so staying in one field is the opposite.

misuse.text: She gave an itinerant speech that went on for hours.
misuse.why: Itinerant describes moving around for work, not speaking at length; use 'long' or 'rambling'.

synonyms.vs: Travelling is everyday and need not involve work; itinerant is formal and suggests moving from place to place for work.
Nomadic describes whole peoples who move with their herds; itinerant is more about individual workers.
Wandering suggests aimless movement; itinerant implies a purpose, such as finding work.

confusables.note: An itinerary is the planned route or schedule of a journey.

origin: From Latin iter, 'journey, way'.

definition: To officially clear someone of blame or guilt for something.
nuance: Exonerate is used when evidence or an inquiry shows that someone was not to blame. It is common in law, journalism and official reports, often in the passive: 'he was exonerated'. It is stronger than 'forgive': it says the person did nothing wrong, or much less than was claimed.

examples.text: New DNA evidence exonerated the man, who had spent twenty years in prison for a crime he did not commit.
The inquiry exonerated the pilot, finding that the crash was caused by a fault in the engine.
The camera footage exonerates him completely: you can see he was nowhere near the shop.
The review exonerates the early researchers, arguing that they could not have known the risks with the tools of the time.
Only the housekeeper's letter could exonerate her, and she had burned it years ago.
Defence lawyers rely on forensic science not only to convict the guilty but also to exonerate the innocent.

cloze.text: The new witness could ___ the accused by proving he was in another city at the time of the crime.
The report ___ the nurse of any blame for the patient's death, saying she had followed every rule.
He hoped the investigation would ___ him and restore his name after months of accusations.

misuse.text: The evidence exonerated the burglar, since his fingerprints were on every window.
misuse.why: Exonerate means to clear of blame; fingerprints on every window would prove guilt, not clear him.

misuse.text: He exonerated the winner with a gold medal.
misuse.why: Exonerate means to clear someone of blame; it has nothing to do with rewarding someone.

synonyms.vs: Acquit is a court's formal verdict of not guilty; exonerate can come from any inquiry or evidence and says the person was truly blameless.
Absolve is to free from guilt or blame, often morally or by authority; exonerate rests on evidence.
Vindicate proves someone or their view was right; exonerate clears them of blame.

origin: From Latin exonerare, 'to unload', from onus, 'burden': to lift the burden of blame.

definition: Happening in repeating cycles, so that the same pattern comes round again and again.
nuance: Cyclical describes processes, trends and histories that repeat in a pattern, such as seasons or booms and busts. In economics, 'cyclical' industries rise and fall with the economy. It differs from 'circular', which is about shape or about an argument that goes back to its start.

examples.text: Farming follows a cyclical pattern: planting, growth, harvest and rest come round again every year.
Economists describe the housing market as cyclical, with long booms followed by sharp falls and recoveries.
My motivation is totally cyclical; a month of working hard, then a month of doing nothing.
Ski resorts depend on cyclical demand, with their busiest period every winter.
The old woman believed that history was cyclical, and that the same mistakes would return in every age.
Ancient calendars were often based on cyclical movements of the moon and stars.

cloze.text: The seasons follow a ___ pattern: spring, summer, autumn and winter, then spring once more.
Economists say that recessions are ___, since good years and bad years keep taking turns.
Some thinkers view history as ___, a series of rises and falls that repeat over centuries.

misuse.text: The cyclical road goes straight from the town to the coast.
misuse.why: Cyclical describes patterns that repeat over time, not the shape of a road.

misuse.text: The cyclical change happened just once and never again.
misuse.why: Cyclical change repeats; a single event is not a cycle.

synonyms.vs: Recurring says only that something comes back; cyclical suggests a regular pattern of stages.
Periodic means happening at intervals, not necessarily in a full pattern.
Seasonal ties the repetition to times of year; cyclical can have longer or irregular cycles.

confusables.note: Circular describes a round shape, or an argument that returns to its start; cyclical is about repetition over time.

origin: From Greek kyklos, 'circle, wheel'.

sense: the ability to prepare for the future
definition: The ability to see what will be needed in the future and to prepare for it.
nuance: Foresight is approving: it is sensible preparation for what is likely, not magic prediction. It often appears as 'lack of foresight' when a disaster could have been avoided. It is common in business, politics and planning.

examples.text: She had the foresight to pack umbrellas, so we stayed dry when everyone else got soaked.
Critics blamed the flooding on the council's lack of foresight in failing to build better drains.
Good policy requires foresight, since decisions about energy today shape the economy decades from now.
The founders showed remarkable foresight by saving a fifth of every year's profit.
Had he possessed a little foresight, he would have noticed that the bridge was rotten.
Historians have praised her foresight in training doctors before the epidemic began.

cloze.text: Thanks to her ___, she had saved money for a rainy day long before the factory closed.
The disaster showed a complete lack of ___: no one had asked what would happen if the river flooded.
He had the ___ to book the tickets months in advance, before the prices rose.

misuse.text: With great foresight, she explained what had happened the day before.
misuse.why: Foresight is about preparing for the future, not looking back at the past; that would be hindsight.

misuse.text: He admired her foresight in solving yesterday's crossword.
misuse.why: Foresight is the ability to anticipate and prepare for what is coming, not skill at solving puzzles.

synonyms.vs: Forethought is careful thinking beforehand about what to do; foresight adds the ability to see what will probably happen.
Vision is a larger picture of the future; foresight is practical preparation.
Prudence means careful, cautious judgement about risk; foresight is anticipating what is coming.

definition: A major piece of work, especially a musical composition or a large piece of writing.
nuance: Opus names a work of art, most often a musical composition, and composers number their works (opus 27). 'Magnum opus' means someone's greatest work. It is also used with humour for a long piece of writing that someone is very proud of.

examples.text: Beethoven's Moonlight sonata is listed as opus 27, number 2, in the catalogue of his work.
My brother has been writing his opus, a fantasy novel of nine hundred pages, for six years.
The composer premiered her latest opus, a piece for choir and orchestra, in Vienna last night.
The festival will premiere three new opuses by young composers, each lasting under ten minutes.
He spent forty winters on his great opus, a history of the valley that nobody would ever read.
Scholars treat the late quartet as the crowning opus of the composer's final years.

cloze.text: Composers number their works, so Brahms's first symphony is catalogued as ___ 68.
She called her sprawling final novel her magnum ___, the greatest work of her life.
The conductor announced that the next ___ would be a short piece for solo violin by a living composer.

misuse.text: The opus of the garden was full of flowers and butterflies.
misuse.why: An opus is a creative work such as a piece of music or a book, not a place.

misuse.text: He composed ten opus in his career.
misuse.why: Opus is singular; several works are 'opuses' (or the Latin 'opera').

synonyms.vs: Work is the everyday word for any creation; opus is formal and usually means a musical piece or a major work.
Composition covers any piece of music or writing; opus stresses a numbered or major work.
Masterpiece means an outstanding work; opus carries no praise unless it is 'magnum opus'.

confusables.note: Opera is a drama set to music; it is also the Latin plural of opus.

origin: From Latin opus, 'work'.

sense: different from the usual or traditional
definition: Different from what is usual, accepted or traditional, especially in methods or opinions.
nuance: Unorthodox describes methods, ideas and lifestyles that depart from tradition. It is neutral: it can be admiring or doubtful, depending on whether the result works. It is wider than 'orthodox' in religion and is often used of teachers, doctors and managers.

examples.text: She has an unorthodox way of studying: she learns her notes by singing them in the shower.
The coach's unorthodox tactics, playing without a striker, baffled opponents and won the league.
Darwin's theory seemed unorthodox in his day because it challenged the widely accepted view that species never changed.
The surgeon used an unorthodox technique that was later adopted by hospitals across the country.
The headmistress, famous for her unorthodox methods, held lessons in the woods whatever the weather.
Few journals would publish such unorthodox views before the 1990s.

cloze.text: Instead of the usual textbook approach, the teacher used an ___ method and let pupils plan their own lessons.
His ___ lifestyle, living on a boat and working only in summer, puzzled his more conventional relatives.
Although the treatment was ___, breaking with standard medical practice, it worked.

misuse.text: The unorthodox method was the one every school had used for a hundred years.
misuse.why: Unorthodox means not following the traditional way, so a century-old method is the opposite.

misuse.text: He was unorthodox, always following the rules exactly.
misuse.why: Unorthodox people break from convention; strictly following the rules is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Unconventional is the everyday word; unorthodox is slightly more formal and stresses breaking from accepted method or belief.
Eccentric is about odd personal behaviour; unorthodox is about methods or opinions.
Maverick describes an independent person who refuses to follow the group; unorthodox describes the way of doing things.

origin: From Greek orthodoxos, 'having the right opinion', from orthos, 'straight, correct', and doxa, 'opinion'.

sense: wander away from the main subject
definition: To wander away from the main subject while speaking or writing.
nuance: Digress is used of speakers and writers who stray from their topic, usually briefly and often before returning to it. It is not always negative: a digression can add colour. The phrase 'but I digress' is a common way to return to the point.

examples.text: Sorry, I digress; where was I? Ah yes, the train was late again.
The author digresses into a long discussion of music, which interrupts the argument but adds colour.
The speaker kept digressing into stories about his childhood, and the audience began to check their watches.
Please do not digress; the meeting must finish by noon and several items remain.
My grandfather digressed whenever he told a story, and each tale led to three others before the end.
Students who digress too often lose the thread of their argument and confuse their readers.

cloze.text: The lecturer began to ___ and spent ten minutes on a story about his dog, before returning to the lesson.
To keep the essay focused, resist the urge to ___ into interesting side issues that are not part of your argument.
She ___ so often during the talk that the audience forgot what the original question had been.

misuse.text: He digressed his speech by repeating the same point five times.
misuse.why: Digress means wandering to another subject; repeating one point is not digressing, and digress takes no object.

misuse.text: The speaker digressed, keeping strictly to his topic.
misuse.why: To digress is to leave the main topic, the opposite of keeping to it.

synonyms.vs: Stray is everyday and covers wandering in general; digress is formal and about speech or writing.
Ramble means talking at length with no clear direction and is critical; digress means leaving the point, often briefly.
Diverge means separating into different paths or views; digress is about speakers leaving their topic.

confusables.note: Regress means to return to an earlier or worse state.

origin: From Latin digredi, 'to step away', from dis-, 'apart', and gradi, 'to step'.

definition: To accept something or agree to it without protest, although you may not really want to.
nuance: Acquiesce suggests reluctant or passive agreement, often because it is easier or because you have no power. It is usually followed by 'in' or 'to'. Critical writers use it for people who fail to resist something wrong.

examples.text: I didn't really want to see another action film, but I acquiesced because everyone else was keen.
The council finally acquiesced to residents' demands and agreed to close the road to heavy lorries.
Historians ask why so many ordinary citizens acquiesced in the new regime instead of resisting it.
The tenants acquiesced in the landlord's proposal, though they privately thought the rent was too high.
She sighed, shrugged and acquiesce, as she always did when her mother used that tone.
By acquiescing to unfair rules without protest, people allow them to become accepted as normal.

cloze.text: He did not agree with the plan, but rather than argue, he ___ and went along with it.
After weeks of pressure from her family, she reluctantly ___ and signed the papers.
A leader who ___ to every demand soon finds that no one respects his authority.

misuse.text: The workers acquiesced loudly by going on strike.
misuse.why: Acquiesce means to accept quietly; going on strike is active resistance.

misuse.text: She acquiesced the offer with delight and shouted 'Yes!'
misuse.why: Acquiesce is passive, reluctant acceptance and takes 'in' or 'to'; eager acceptance is not acquiescence.

synonyms.vs: Comply means to obey a rule or order; acquiesce means to accept without objection something you may dislike.
Consent is willing, often formal agreement; acquiesce is more passive and reluctant.
Submit means to yield to a stronger force; acquiesce is quieter and may be a choice.

confusables.note: Acquit means to declare someone not guilty.

origin: From Latin acquiescere, 'to rest', from quies, 'rest'.

definition: To criticise someone severely and formally for something they have done.
nuance: Censure is formal: usually an official body such as a parliament, council or professional board states strong disapproval of someone's conduct. It is also a noun, as in 'a vote of censure'. Do not confuse it with 'censor', which is about removing material.

examples.text: Parliament voted to censure the minister for misleading the public about the cost of the project.
The medical board censured the doctor and warned that any further breach would lead to suspension.
Moralists of the period censured novel-reading as a waste of time, especially for young women.
The school censured him in front of everyone, and he's still embarrassed about it.
The old priest was quick to censure anyone who laughed in church.
Critics who censure the novel for its length overlook how much of the plot depends on those details.

cloze.text: The council voted to ___ the mayor for using public money on private trips, though it did not remove him.
The professional body decided to ___ the lawyer, placing a public record of its disapproval on her file.
It is unfair to ___ a writer for failing to do something that he never set out to do.

misuse.text: The editor censured the article, cutting out all the political lines.
misuse.why: That describes censoring; censure means to criticise severely, not to remove material.

misuse.text: The teacher censured the pupil with a gold star.
misuse.why: Censure means to criticise severely, so it cannot be a reward.

synonyms.vs: Criticise is everyday and can be mild; censure is formal and severe, often by an official body.
Condemn is strong disapproval of something wrong, not always official; censure often means a formal rebuke.
Reprimand is a formal telling-off by a superior; censure can come from a group or the public.

confusables.note: Censor means to remove or ban material thought unacceptable.

origin: From Latin censura, 'judgement', from censere, 'to assess'.

sense: a stale, obvious remark said as if wise
definition: A remark that is dull and obvious because it has been used so often, though said as if it were wise.
nuance: Platitude is critical: it names a comfortable saying such as 'time heals all wounds' offered when real thought or help is needed. It is common in reviews and criticism of speeches. The speaker may mean well, but the remark adds nothing.

examples.text: All I got were platitudes like 'everything happens for a reason', when what I wanted was real advice.
The president's speech was full of platitudes about hope and unity but contained no new policy.
Good essays avoid platitudes, such as 'education is important', and make specific claims that can be argued with evidence.
The review dismissed the report as a collection of platitudes that told the committee nothing new.
He murmured a platitude about time healing all wounds, and she wanted to throw her tea at him.
Calling a complex problem a matter of common sense is a platitude that explains nothing.

cloze.text: Instead of real comfort, the visitor offered the usual ___ that 'time heals all wounds'.
The speech was a string of empty ___ about hard work and teamwork, with no actual plan.
Marking essays, she circled every ___ that sounded wise but said nothing, such as 'life is full of surprises'.

misuse.text: His wise and original platitude changed how the whole country thought about justice.
misuse.why: A platitude is a dull, obvious remark; a wise and original idea is the opposite.

misuse.text: She wore a beautiful platitude on her wedding day.
misuse.why: A platitude is a stale remark, not an object or an outfit.

synonyms.vs: A cliche is any overused phrase or idea, including in style; a platitude is an overused remark presented as wise.
A truism is an obviously true statement and may be harmless; a platitude is stale and used instead of thinking.
Banality is the dullness itself; a platitude is the remark that shows it.

confusables.note: Latitude sounds similar; it means freedom of action, or a position north or south of the equator.

origin: From French plat, 'flat': a flat, dull remark.

sense: a forceful one-sided attack in writing or speech
definition: A forceful written or spoken attack that argues strongly against someone else's beliefs or policies.
nuance: A polemic is a passionate, one-sided argument aimed at winning, not at weighing both sides. It can be praised as powerful writing or criticised as unfair. The adjective is 'polemical', and the word is common in book and article reviews.

examples.text: Her book is less a balanced study than a polemic against the education system, hammering one point on every page.
The columnist's latest polemic accuses the government of ignoring the countryside, and it has angered ministers.
He started with a simple question about parking and ended up delivering a ten-minute polemic against the council.
The editor rejected the article because it was a polemic rather than a reasoned analysis of the evidence.
The pamphlet was a fiery polemic against the landlords, and men read it aloud in the tavern by candlelight.
Eighteenth-century polemics against the church often mixed serious argument with open mockery.

cloze.text: The article is not a balanced review but a one-sided ___ against the new tax, and it never mentions any argument in its favour.
Her book began as a calm study but turned into a fierce ___ against the whole industry.
In his pamphlet, a passionate ___ aimed at winning supporters rather than weighing evidence, he attacked every critic by name.

misuse.text: The polemic was a calm, balanced survey that gave equal space to both sides.
misuse.why: A polemic is a forceful one-sided attack, the opposite of a balanced survey.

misuse.text: The essay had a polemic tone.
misuse.why: Polemic is a noun for the attack itself; the adjective is 'polemical'.

synonyms.vs: Diatribe is a bitter, angry speech or text, often abusive; polemic argues a case, even if one-sidedly.
Tirade is a long, angry outburst, usually spoken; polemic is more organised and usually written.
A manifesto announces aims and principles; a polemic mainly attacks opponents.

origin: From Greek polemikos, 'warlike', from polemos, 'war'.

definition: To officially cancel a decision, or to put an end to something firmly, often by force.
nuance: Quash has two main uses. In law, a court quashes a verdict or decision by cancelling it. More generally, you quash a rebellion, rumour or hope by putting a decisive stop to it.

examples.text: Troops moved in to quash the uprising within days, arresting its leaders and closing the roads.
The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction after new evidence showed that a witness had lied.
Authoritarian regimes often quash dissent by closing newspapers and jailing critics.
She tried to quash the rumour before it reached the whole school.
With one cold look, the captain quashed the sailors' hopes of an early return.
Historians debate whether the decree was meant to quash religious debate or simply to regulate it.

cloze.text: The government sent in the army to ___ the rebellion before it could spread to other cities.
Lawyers asked the higher court to ___ the verdict, arguing that the trial had been unfair.
The company issued a firm statement to ___ rumours that it was about to close.

misuse.text: The court quashed his conviction, so he must stay in prison.
misuse.why: To quash a conviction is to cancel it, which would free him, not keep him in prison.

misuse.text: She quashed the soft pillow flat to make it comfortable.
misuse.why: Quash means to suppress or officially cancel something, not to press a physical object flat; for that use 'squash' or 'flatten'.

phrases: The court quashed the ruling on...

synonyms.vs: Suppress is wider and is used for feelings and information too; quash stresses stopping something decisively.
Overturn is the general word for reversing a decision; quash is the legal term and also means crushing a revolt.
Crush is informal and physical; quash is more formal and often legal or political.

confusables.note: Squash means to press flat or crush physically; quash is for ideas, rumours, revolts and decisions.

sense: perfectly typical, like the original model
definition: Being a perfect, typical example of its kind, like the original model for all the others.
nuance: Archetypal describes a person, character or event that is the perfect, typical example of its kind, as if it were the original model. It is common in literary criticism, psychology and film reviews. It is usually neutral or approving and does not suggest an unfair stereotype.

examples.text: Critics called the film's hero the archetypal lone cowboy, riding in from nowhere to save the town.
Jung believed that archetypal figures, such as the hero and the wise old man, appear in myths across cultures.
She's the archetypal big sister: bossy, protective and always right.
He was the archetypal absent-minded professor, with chalk on his sleeves and two different socks.
The museum's collection includes archetypal examples of every major style of Greek pottery.
Scholars of folklore identify the cruel stepmother as an archetypal character in fairy tales.

cloze.text: With her red hood and basket, she is the ___ fairy-tale child walking alone into the dark forest.
He was the ___ self-made man: born poor, working from dawn and building his business from nothing.
Folklorists study ___ characters such as the trickster, who appear in the stories of many different cultures.

misuse.text: The archetypal hero of the story was a very unusual and unique man unlike anyone else.
misuse.why: Archetypal means perfectly typical, the pattern others copy, so it clashes with being unusual and unique.

misuse.text: The archetypal answer to the maths question was 42, and every other answer was wrong.
misuse.why: Archetypal means a typical, original pattern; for a correct answer use 'right' or 'correct'.

synonyms.vs: Classic is everyday and can mean simply excellent; archetypal means the model that others copy.
Quintessential means the purest example of a quality; archetypal means the original pattern others follow.
Typical is plain and just means usual; archetypal suggests a perfect, model example.

confusables.note: Stereotypical suggests an oversimplified, often unfair picture; archetypal suggests a deep, lasting pattern.

origin: From Greek arkhe, 'first', and typos, 'pattern' or 'mould'.

sense: so ordinary and overused that it is dull
definition: So ordinary, predictable and overused that it is dull and shows no originality.
nuance: Banal describes remarks, ideas, plots and art that are so ordinary and overused that they are boring. It is always critical and is common in reviews and essays on style. A banal comment is not wrong, just unoriginal.

examples.text: The film's banal dialogue, full of clichés like 'time heals all wounds', made the audience groan.
Orwell warned that banal, ready-made phrases save writers the effort of thinking.
Our chat was so banal: the weather, the traffic and what we'd had for lunch.
He offered a banal greeting, the same polite words he said to everyone he met.
The reviewer dismissed the proposal as banal, offering nothing that experts had not already said.
Greetings cards often use banal verses that people copy without noticing how overused they are.

cloze.text: The speech was full of ___ remarks, such as 'We must all work together', that everyone had heard a thousand times.
After the brilliant first novel, the sequel was a disappointment: dull, predictable and ___.
She wanted a wedding toast that avoided the ___, overused jokes that every best man tells.

misuse.text: His banal invention was so original that nobody had ever seen anything like it.
misuse.why: Banal means unoriginal and overused, so it clashes with something completely original.

misuse.text: She wore a banal gown covered in jewels that stunned the whole room.
misuse.why: Banal means ordinary and dull; a stunning jewelled gown is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Trite is used for remarks that were once meaningful but are now stale; banal stresses dullness and lack of originality.
Hackneyed means worn out by overuse, mostly of phrases and images; banal is wider.
Commonplace can be neutral, meaning ordinary; banal is always critical.

confusables.note: Baneful means harmful or poisonous.

definition: Eager to argue or fight, and quick to challenge or oppose other people.
nuance: Combative describes people, styles and moods that are ready to argue or fight. It is mildly to strongly critical, though in politics or law it can be approved as spirited. It is mostly about words and attitude rather than physical violence.

examples.text: The combative senator interrupted every question and accused reporters of lying.
He's in a combative mood today, so I'd avoid mentioning the budget.
Combative debates can sharpen ideas, but they may also stop people from listening to each other.
She lifted her chin in a combative way, daring him to disagree.
The chairman asked members to avoid a combative tone and to address the issues calmly.
The author's combative style suits a book written to challenge the established view.

cloze.text: Always ready to argue, he gave a ___ reply to even the friendliest question.
The ___ lawyer attacked every witness, refusing to accept a single answer without a challenge.
The talks began in a ___ mood, with each side ready to fight over every word.

misuse.text: The combative child sat quietly and agreed with everything that anyone said.
misuse.why: Combative means eager to argue or fight, so someone who agrees with everything is not combative.

misuse.text: She was combative because she was generous with her time and money.
misuse.why: Combative is about readiness to fight or argue, not generosity.

synonyms.vs: Belligerent is angrier and more threatening; combative is ready to argue and challenge, sometimes with energy.
Argumentative is everyday and about disputing; combative suggests a stronger fighting spirit.
